title: Extension for workers' comp review
full_text:
The Minns government has extended part of its review of NSW's workers compensation scheme after being hit with a deluge of submissions from the construction industry and other sectors with the most at stake.
The review is evaluating how the state's Nominal Insurer scheme, which covers more than 340,000 employers, could be overhauled. This followed earlier reforms - including higher thresholds for psychological injury claims - and an 18-month freeze on premium collection rates.
Of the nearly 550 submissions received, 50 per cent came from medium to large employers and 46 per cent from small businesses. Construction accounted for nearly a quarter of all respondents, the largest response from any one sector. There were also numerous submissions from the health and community services, manufacturing and retail sectors.
Employers overwhelmingly called for greater premium predictability and a framework that rewarded positive workplace safety cultures. As a result, the state government has extended the review to November 8.
The extension was a signal that the government intended to pursue further reform if Labor retained power in next March's state election.
Master Builders NSW executive director Matt Pollock said the current regime disproportionately hurt small builders and discouraged apprenticeship hiring. Because construction carries higher physical risks, the sector faces steep industry-wide premium benchmarks. Pollock advocated for weighting premiums towards individual company safety records rather than penalising the whole industry.
"The safety of a business should be reflected in premiums to provide effective incentives to employers with a good safety culture," he said.
"More certainty around the size of premiums is especially important for small construction firms which often struggle to manage pressure on cash flow."
High premiums compound cash flow problems for builders. ASIC data for the September quarter revealed nearly 900 insolvencies in the NSW construction sector - the highest on record.
